extracted.intended_audience: patent professionals, IP policymakers, researchers and statisticians working with patent data
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, examination standards, procedural rules and data-comparability cautions used in evaluating patent applications, grants, families, PCT filings, utility models and patents-in-force in a global statistical context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent offices must assess whether the claims made in applications meet the standards of novelty, non-obviousness and industrial applicability defined in national laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the substantive legal standards applied during examination; because they are defined in national laws, their interpretation and application can vary across offices, affecting grant rates and international comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal and substantive examination before grant
rubrics_metrics.description: Offices carry out a formal and substantive examination before deciding whether to issue a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The procedure for granting a patent varies between offices; differences in examination capacity and procedural delays affect the numbers of patents granted and make direct cross-office comparisons difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent term length
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent rights generally last for up to 20 years from the date an application is filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actual duration depends on maintenance/renewal payments and jurisdictions; statistics show variation in how many patents remain in force for seven years or the full 20 years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintenance/renewal fees and lapse
rubrics_metrics.description: Holders must pay maintenance/renewal fees to maintain the validity of their patents, and may opt to let a patent lapse before the end of its full term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents in force counts reflect whether fees are paid; opting not to pay causes patents to lapse and reduces the count of patents in force over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility model eligibility and characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: A utility model is a special form of patent right granted by a state or jurisdiction for a fixed period of time; terms and conditions differ slightly from those for normal patents, including a shorter term of protection and less stringent eligibility requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offices treat utility models differently (eligibility, term), so utility model statistics and trends are distinct from standard patent statistics (example: large share of global utility model filings concentrated at China’s office).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of pending applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Pending applications are all patent applications, at any stage in the process, awaiting a final decision by a patent office, including those applications for which applicants have not filed a request for examination (where applicable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to estimate backlog and workload; pending-application counts vary by office and are affected by procedural requirements such as request-for-examination systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of foreign-oriented patent family
rubrics_metrics.description: A foreign-related (foreign-oriented) patent family is one in which the filing office differs from the office of the applicant's country of origin; such families can include only one filing office when applicants choose to file only with a foreign office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a Canadian applicant filing directly with the USPTO without a prior Canadian filing results in a foreign-oriented patent family with just one office. This definition affects counting and classification of patent families across origins and offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: PCT filing purpose and limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) allows applicants to seek patent protection for an invention simultaneously in a large number of countries by filing a single PCT international application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PCT simplifies centralized filing, but the granting of patents remains under the control of national and regional patent offices and is carried out in the 'national phase' or 'regional phase'—the PCT itself does not grant patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination outcome categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent examination outcomes for applications processed are categorized as granted, rejected, or withdrawn/abandoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proportions of each outcome vary considerably across offices (e.g., high withdrawal/abandonment rates in some countries; high grant rates in others), reflecting differences in procedure, applicant behaviour and examination practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resident vs non-resident composition and importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent statistics distinguish resident and non-resident applications and grants; the composition (share of resident vs non-resident) affects interpretation of office-level counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, more than half of patents in force in the U.S. originated from non-resident applicants, while resident applicants account for the bulk in other jurisdictions. See glossary for formal definitions used in the dataset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents in force (definition and interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents in force are patents that remain valid (typically because required maintenance/renewal fees have been paid) across jurisdictions at a given date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents in force are used as a stock measure; counts and average ages vary by office and reflect historical filing behaviour and renewal decisions (e.g., estimates of patents in force and average ages by country are provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal comparability caution (applications vs grants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Application data for a given year should not be compared with grant data from the same year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a time lag between filing and grant because examination can be lengthy; comparing different-year measures without adjusting for lag can lead to misleading conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological comparability warnings (office-specific breaks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in methodology at an office can create breaks in time series and affect comparability (example: China's pre-2017 data are not comparable due to a change in methodology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Users must heed office-specific methodological notes when interpreting trends and computing growth rates; WIPO includes such notes in its dataset descriptions.
